modules.name: Abs
modules.header:
The magnitude of a floating-point value, by clearing the sign bit.
Not a comparison against zero, which is the obvious implementation and the wrong one: it has to decide what
to do about the two zeros and about a NaN, and every answer it can give is a special case. Clearing the bit
has no special cases at all — both zeros become `+0.0`, both infinities become positive, and a NaN keeps
being a NaN with its payload intact — and it is exact for every argument.

modules.name: Angle
modules.header:
Converting between degrees and radians.
Each direction scales by the nearest representable value of its constant rather than dividing by the other
one, so `DegToRad(180.0)` is exactly `Pi` and the round trip does not drift. Signed zeros and infinities
keep their signs, and a NaN stays a NaN.

modules.name: ArcCos
modules.header:
The inverse cosine, over the closed interval its argument is defined on.
Built from `ArcSin`'s kernel rather than computed separately, which is what keeps the two consistent with
each other near the endpoints, where a small disagreement between them is most visible. The result is in
`[0, Pi]`, and an argument outside `[-1, 1]` is a NaN rather than a clamped answer.

modules.name: ArcCot
modules.header:
The inverse cotangent, over the whole real line.
Written against `ArcTan` and the reciprocal rather than as `Pi/2 - ArcTan(x)`, so the answer near zero — where
the cotangent is large and the subtraction would cancel — keeps its precision. The result is in `[0, Pi]`,
with the infinities mapping to the endpoints.

modules.name: ArcHyperbolic
modules.header:
The inverse hyperbolic functions, each written to avoid the cancellation its closed form invites. Every one of them
is a logarithm of something built from a square root, and every one of those expressions loses the answer somewhere:
`log(x + sqrt(x*x + 1))` cancels for a negative argument and overflows the square root long before the answer would
overflow, `log(x + sqrt(x*x - 1))` cancels as the argument approaches one from above, and
`0.5 * log((1 + x) / (1 - x))` cancels as the argument approaches zero. So each is split into ranges, with `Log1p`
doing the work near zero, where its whole reason for existing applies. Accuracy: error at most 2 ulps in each - one
from the logarithm and one from what is fed to it.

modules.name: ArcSin
modules.header:
The inverse sine, over the closed interval its argument is defined on.
A rational approximation on the lower half of the range and a square-root identity on the upper half, which
is what avoids the derivative going to infinity at the endpoints. The result is in `[-Pi/2, Pi/2]`, and an
argument outside `[-1, 1]` is a NaN rather than a clamped answer.

modules.name: ArcTan
modules.header:
The inverse tangent of a single value.
The argument is folded into a small interval around zero using the addition formula, and a polynomial does
the rest; the fold is what makes a large argument no less accurate than a small one. The result is in
`[-Pi/2, Pi/2]`, which is half a turn — `ArcTan2` is the one that gives the whole turn and needs two
arguments to do it.

modules.name: ArcTan2
modules.header:
The angle of the point (x, y), which is what an inverse tangent is usually actually wanted for.
`ArcTan(y / x)` cannot answer this and no accuracy improves it: the division throws away which quadrant the point is
in, so (-1, -1) and (1, 1) become the same argument and the same answer, and a point on the vertical axis divides by
zero. Taking the two coordinates separately keeps the quadrant, gives the full turn rather than half of it, and has
an answer everywhere except the origin — where, by the convention every implementation follows, it returns zero
rather than refusing.
**Accuracy: error at most 2 ulps.** One from the inverse tangent, and one from the quadrant correction, which is
done against Pi carried in two parts so the subtraction near the negative axis does not lose the answer.

modules.name: Bits
modules.header:
The bit-level primitives the rest of the package is built on.
Nothing here is meant to be called from outside it. Both directions are one register-to-register move of a
bit pattern, but which registers those are is the calling convention's business, so each architecture writes
its own pair.

modules.name: Cbrt
modules.header:
The real cube root.
Defined for every real argument, unlike the square root, because a negative number has a real cube root; the
sign is carried through rather than being a special case. A bit-pattern estimate seeds two Newton steps.
Error at most one ulp.

modules.name: Ceil
modules.header:
Rounding toward positive infinity.
By exponent inspection rather than by adding and subtracting a large constant, so it is exact for every
argument including those too large to have a fractional part at all. A value strictly between negative one
and zero becomes `-0.0` rather than `+0.0`, which is what IEEE 754 requires and what a caller dividing by
the result will notice.

modules.name: Classify
modules.header:
What a floating-point value is, before any arithmetic is done to it.
IEEE 754 sorts every bit pattern into five kinds, and most of the bugs in floating-point code come from
treating one as another: a NaN mistaken for a number because a comparison against it was false, a signed
zero whose sign a comparison threw away, a subnormal treated as zero because it printed as one. So the
questions here are answered by bit pattern wherever a comparison would lie, and the sign of a zero is
preserved rather than normalized away.
The neighbourhood operations — `NextAfter`, `NextUp`, `NextDown`, `UlpDistance` — are here for the same
reason: they are about the representation rather than about the value, and they are how a test says two
results are within an ulp of each other.

modules.name: Const
modules.header:
The mathematical constants, each rounded once to the nearest `float64`.
Written as decimal literals rather than computed, so no expression's rounding stands between the true value
and the stored one. A `float32` caller converts, which rounds a second time and is still the nearest
`float32` to the true constant for every value here.

modules.name: Cos
modules.header:
The cosine of an angle in radians.
Argument reduction against Pi carried in enough parts to be exact, then the shared kernel in `Trig.rux`. The
reduction is the whole difficulty: a naive one loses a bit of the answer for every bit the argument grows,
so a large angle would be meaningless. Error at most one ulp for every finite argument; an infinity is a NaN.

modules.name: Cosh
modules.header:
The hyperbolic cosine.
Three ranges: near zero the exponential is written so the leading one survives, in the middle it is the
average of `Exp(x)` and its reciprocal, and at the top only the growing term is left and the other has
underflowed. The result is at least one, and both infinities give positive infinity.

modules.name: Cotan
modules.header:
The cotangent of an angle in radians.
The reciprocal is computed inside the kernel rather than as `1 / Tan(x)`, which would round twice and lose
the answer near a pole. A signed zero maps to an infinity of the same sign; an infinite argument is a NaN,
since the cotangent has no limit there.

modules.name: Cotanh
modules.header:
The hyperbolic cotangent.
The reciprocal of `Tanh`, computed through the same expression rather than as a division of it, so the
approach to `±1` at large arguments does not cost a rounding. A signed zero maps to an infinity of the same
sign, and the infinities map to `-1` and `1`.

modules.name: Exp
modules.header:
exp(hi - lo) * 2^k, for a reduced argument |hi - lo| <= 0.5*ln2 whose leading part is hi. Keeping hi and lo apart
rather than passing their sum is what carries the last bits: the sum has already rounded, and near the ends of the
reduction that rounding is the whole error.
Exp2 reaches the same reduced form by a different route and shares this.

modules.name: Exp2
modules.header:
Two raised to a power.
Reduces to the same form `Exp` uses and shares its scaled kernel, but reaches it by splitting the argument
at the binary point instead of dividing by the logarithm of two — which is why an integer exponent in range
is exact here and only nearly exact through `Exp`. Error at most one ulp.

modules.name: Expm1
modules.header:
The exponential, minus one, without the cancellation that subtraction invites.
`Exp(x) - 1` loses everything for a small `x`: the exponential rounds to a number near one, and subtracting
one throws away all the bits that were the answer. This computes the difference directly, so the relative
error stays at one ulp as the argument approaches zero. That is the whole reason the function exists, and
it is what `Log1p` is the inverse of.

modules.name: Floor
modules.header:
Rounding toward negative infinity.
By exponent inspection rather than by adding and subtracting a large constant, so it is exact for every
argument including those too large to have a fractional part. A NaN or an infinity passes through unchanged.

modules.name: Hypot
modules.header:
The length of the hypotenuse, without overflowing on the way.
`Sqrt(x*x + y*y)` is the definition and not the implementation: either square overflows for arguments whose
answer is perfectly representable, and underflows to zero for arguments whose answer is not zero. Scaling by
the larger operand first removes both, at the cost of one extra rounding.

modules.name: Integer
modules.header:
Integer arithmetic with a mathematical flavour: magnitude, ordering, and the number-theory pair.
Everything here is generic over the integer type in the same way `Core`'s checked arithmetic is, and for the same
reason: an integer's zero, its signedness and its two limits all follow from one operand, so `int8` and `uint512`
run the same code and no width can be forgotten. Nothing here is written per width.
The operations that can fail say so by returning `true`, matching `AddChecked` and its family exactly. That
convention reads backwards the first time - `true` means the answer is not the true one - but a family that
disagrees with itself about which way the flag points is far worse than one that is uniformly surprising.
Where an operation can fail, it is because the two's-complement range is not symmetric: the most negative value of
every signed width has no positive counterpart, so its magnitude, its negation and its greatest common divisor with
zero are all unrepresentable. That one asymmetry is behind nearly every edge case below.

modules.name: Log
modules.header:
The natural logarithm.
The exponent gives the integer part and a polynomial in the reduced mantissa gives the rest, which is the
shape every logarithm here uses. Error at most one ulp. Zero is negative infinity, a negative argument is a
NaN, and `Log1p` is the one to use when the argument is near one.

modules.name: Log10
modules.header:
The base-ten logarithm.
Scaled from the natural logarithm with the constant carried in two parts, so the multiplication does not
cost a bit. An exact power of ten in range gives its exponent exactly, which is what a caller counting
digits depends on.

modules.name: Log1p
modules.header:
The logarithm of one plus the argument, without the cancellation that addition invites.
`Log(1 + x)` loses everything for a small `x`: the addition rounds away the bits that were the answer before
the logarithm sees them. This reduces around one directly, so the relative error stays at one ulp as the
argument approaches zero. It is the inverse of `Expm1` and the reason the inverse hyperbolic functions can
be accurate near zero at all.

modules.name: Log2
modules.header:
The base-two logarithm.
The exponent field already holds the integer part, so an exact power of two in range gives its exponent
exactly and without arithmetic; the mantissa supplies the fraction. That exactness is why a caller sizing a
power-of-two allocation should reach for this rather than for a scaled natural logarithm.

modules.name: Max
modules.header:
The larger of two floating-point values, under IEEE 754's rule rather than the comparison's.
`a > b ? a : b` is not this: it answers a NaN whenever the NaN is on the wrong side, and it cannot tell the
two zeros apart. Here a NaN argument is ignored in favour of the other one — two NaNs give a NaN — and
`+0.0` is greater than `-0.0`, which a comparison says is false.

modules.name: Min
modules.header:
The smaller of two floating-point values, under IEEE 754's rule rather than the comparison's.
`a < b ? a : b` is not this: it answers a NaN whenever the NaN is on the wrong side, and it cannot tell the
two zeros apart. Here a NaN argument is ignored in favour of the other one — two NaNs give a NaN — and
`-0.0` is less than `+0.0`, which a comparison says is false.

modules.name: Mod
modules.header:
The floating-point remainder, which is exact whenever it is defined.
Computed by repeated scaled subtraction rather than through a division, so no rounding enters and the result
is the true remainder rather than the nearest representable one. The sign follows the dividend, as C's
`fmod` does. A zero divisor or an infinite dividend has no remainder and gives a NaN.

modules.name: Pow
modules.header:
A power with a floating-point exponent.
A logarithm and an exponential, with the special cases decided first because there are more of them here
than anywhere else in the package: every combination of zero, one, the infinities and a NaN has an answer
IEEE 754 names, and several of them are surprising — `Pow(1.0, NaN)` is one, and `Pow(NaN, 0.0)` is one.
A whole-number exponent should go to `PowInteger`, which is exact wherever an exact answer is representable
and does not return 999.9999999999999 for the cube of ten.

modules.name: PowInteger
modules.header:
A power with an integer exponent, by repeated squaring.
Accuracy: error at most one ulp per squaring, so about log2(|n|) ulps in the worst case — and exactly zero
whenever every intermediate is representable. That exactness is the reason to have this beside `Pow`, which goes
through a logarithm and an exponential and so returns 999.9999999999999 for a cube of ten as readily as 1000. A
caller raising a value to a whole number almost always wants the exact answer where one exists.
The sign rules are decided by the exponent's parity rather than derived from a logarithm, so a negative base is
ordinary here where `Pow` has to work to make it meaningful at all.

modules.name: Round
modules.header:
Rounding to the nearest integral value, with halfway cases going away from zero.
The rule a person means by "round", and not the rule the hardware uses: IEEE 754 arithmetic rounds halfway
cases to even, which `RoundTiesToEven` in `Rounding.rux` provides. Both return a float rather than an
integer, because the answer is not always representable as one.

modules.name: Rounding
modules.header:
Rounding, in every direction anyone means by the word.
`Floor`, `Ceil`, `Trunc` and `Round` already name four of the five directions, each with its own file. What was
missing is the fifth - ties to even, the default IEEE 754 rounds arithmetic with, and the one that keeps a long sum
of rounded values from drifting upward - and a way to name a direction as a value rather than by choosing a
function at the call site.
All five agree on everything except the halfway cases, which is exactly why the halfway cases are what the test
spends its time on. Every one of them returns a float rather than an integer, because the answer is not always
representable as one and quietly saturating would hide that; `ToIntegerChecked` is where the conversion happens, and
it reports rather than guesses.

modules.name: Sin
modules.header:
The sine of an angle in radians.
Argument reduction against Pi carried in enough parts to be exact, then the shared kernel in `Trig.rux`. The
reduction is the whole difficulty: a naive one loses a bit of the answer for every bit the argument grows,
so a large angle would be meaningless. Error at most one ulp for every finite argument; an infinity is a NaN.

modules.name: SinCos
modules.header:
The sine and the cosine of one angle, from one argument reduction.
The reduction is the expensive part and both functions need the same one, so asking for both here costs
little more than asking for either separately — which is what a rotation, a polar conversion or a Fourier
term actually wants. The two results are identical to what `Sin` and `Cos` return for the same argument.

modules.name: Sinh
modules.header:
The hyperbolic sine.
Near zero it goes through `Expm1`, because the closed form subtracts two nearly equal exponentials and loses
everything there; further out the subtraction is harmless and only the growing term survives at the top. Odd,
so a signed zero returns itself and each infinity returns itself.

modules.name: Sqrt
modules.header:
The square root, computed by the hardware instruction.
Correctly rounded — error at most half an ulp — which is not a claim about this code but about the
instruction: IEEE 754 requires it to return the nearest representable value to the true root at every
argument, and every architecture here has one that does, with the special cases already right. The argument
arrives in the register the result is returned in under every convention involved, so the whole body is the
instruction and no ABI override is needed.

modules.name: Tan
modules.header:
The tangent of an angle in radians.
Argument reduction against Pi carried in enough parts to be exact, then the shared kernel in `Trig.rux`. The
reduction matters more here than for sine or cosine: near an odd multiple of `Pi/2` the tangent is enormous
and its value is decided entirely by the low bits of the reduced argument. An infinite argument is a NaN.

modules.name: Tanh
modules.header:
The hyperbolic tangent.
Three ranges: through `Expm1` near zero, where the closed form cancels; the ordinary expression in the
middle; and `±1` at the top, where the true value is within an ulp of it. Odd and bounded, so a signed zero
returns itself and the infinities return `-1` and `1` exactly.

modules.name: Trig
modules.header:
The argument reduction and the polynomial kernels behind Sin, Cos, Tan and Cotan. Nothing here is meant to be called
from outside the package: every kernel carries a precondition on its argument that only the reduction can establish.

modules.name: Trunc
modules.header:
Rounding toward zero: the integral part, with the fraction discarded.
By exponent inspection rather than through a conversion to an integer, so it is exact for every argument
including those larger than any integer type could hold. The sign is kept, so a value strictly between
negative one and zero becomes `-0.0`.

doc.summary: Computes the absolute value of `x`.
doc.markdown:
Computes the absolute value of `x`.
This clears the sign bit rather than comparing with zero. Either signed zero therefore becomes `+0.0`, either
infinity becomes positive infinity, and a NaN remains a NaN.
doc.returns: `x` without its sign

doc.summary: Computes the absolute value of `x` at `float32` precision.
doc.markdown:
Computes the absolute value of `x` at `float32` precision.
Widening a finite `float32` to `float64` and narrowing its magnitude back is exact. As with the wide overload,
either signed zero becomes `+0.0`, either infinity becomes positive infinity, and a NaN remains a NaN.
doc.returns: `x` without its sign

doc.summary: Converts an angle from degrees to radians.
doc.markdown:
Converts an angle from degrees to radians.
The conversion scales by the nearest `float64` to `Pi / 180`, making `DegToRad(180.0)` exactly `Pi`. A signed zero
keeps its sign, infinities keep their sign, and a NaN remains a NaN.
doc.returns: the equivalent angle in radians

doc.summary: Converts an angle from degrees to radians at `float32` precision.
doc.markdown:
Converts an angle from degrees to radians at `float32` precision.
The input widens exactly to `float64`; the wide conversion is then rounded back to `float32`.
doc.returns: the equivalent angle in radians

doc.summary: Converts an angle from radians to degrees.
doc.markdown:
Converts an angle from radians to degrees.
The conversion scales by the nearest `float64` to `180 / Pi`, making `RadToDeg(Pi)` exactly `180.0`. A signed zero
keeps its sign, infinities keep their sign, and a NaN remains a NaN.
doc.returns: the equivalent angle in degrees

doc.summary: Converts an angle from radians to degrees at `float32` precision.
doc.markdown:
Converts an angle from radians to degrees at `float32` precision.
The input widens exactly to `float64`; the wide conversion is then rounded back to `float32`.
doc.returns: the equivalent angle in degrees

doc.summary: Computes the inverse cosine of `x` in radians.
doc.markdown:
Computes the inverse cosine of `x` in radians.
The result lies in `[0, Pi]`: `1.0` maps to zero, either signed zero maps to `Pi / 2`, and `-1.0` maps to `Pi`. An
input outside `[-1, 1]` returns a NaN, and a NaN remains a NaN.
doc.returns: the angle in radians whose cosine is `x`, or a NaN when `x` is outside the function's domain

doc.summary: Computes the inverse cosine of `x` in radians at `float32` precision.
doc.markdown:
Computes the inverse cosine of `x` in radians at `float32` precision.
The input widens exactly to `float64`; the wide result is then rounded back to `float32`.
doc.returns: the angle in radians whose cosine is `x`, or a NaN when `x` is outside the function's domain

doc.summary: Computes the inverse cotangent of `x` in radians.
doc.markdown:
Computes the inverse cotangent of `x` in radians.
The result lies in `[0, Pi]`: positive infinity maps to zero, either signed zero maps to `Pi / 2`, and negative
infinity maps to `Pi`. A NaN remains a NaN.
doc.returns: the angle in radians whose cotangent is `x`

doc.summary: Computes the inverse cotangent of `x` in radians at `float32` precision.
doc.markdown:
Computes the inverse cotangent of `x` in radians at `float32` precision.
The input widens exactly to `float64`; the wide result is then rounded back to `float32`.
doc.returns: the angle in radians whose cotangent is `x`

doc.summary: The inverse hyperbolic sine: the value whose hyperbolic sine is `x`.
doc.markdown:
The inverse hyperbolic sine: the value whose hyperbolic sine is `x`.
Defined for every real argument, odd, and unbounded in both directions. A NaN propagates and an infinity gives an
infinity of the same sign.
doc.returns: the inverse hyperbolic sine of `x`

doc.summary: Computes the inverse hyperbolic sine of `x` at `float32` precision.
doc.markdown: Computes the inverse hyperbolic sine of `x` at `float32` precision.

doc.summary: The inverse hyperbolic cosine: the non-negative value whose hyperbolic cosine is `x`.
doc.markdown:
The inverse hyperbolic cosine: the non-negative value whose hyperbolic cosine is `x`.
Defined only for arguments of one and above; anything below has no real answer and gives a NaN. The result is never
negative, since the hyperbolic cosine is even and this returns the branch above zero.
doc.returns: the non-negative inverse hyperbolic cosine of `x`, or a NaN when `x < 1`

doc.markdown: Computes the inverse hyperbolic cosine of `x` at `float32` precision.

doc.returns: the inverse hyperbolic tangent of `x`, an infinity at either endpoint, or a NaN outside `[-1, 1]`

doc.markdown: Computes the inverse hyperbolic tangent of `x` at `float32` precision.
doc.returns: the inverse hyperbolic tangent of `x`, an infinity at either endpoint, or a NaN outside `[-1, 1]`

doc.summary: Computes the inverse sine of `x` in radians.
doc.markdown:
Computes the inverse sine of `x` in radians.
The result lies in `[-Pi / 2, Pi / 2]`. A signed zero returns itself, either endpoint maps to the matching endpoint
of the result range, an input outside `[-1, 1]` returns a NaN, and a NaN remains a NaN.
doc.returns: the angle in radians whose sine is `x`, or a NaN when `x` is outside the function's domain

doc.markdown: Computes the inverse sine of `x` in radians at `float32` precision.
doc.returns: the angle in radians whose sine is `x`, or a NaN when `x` is outside the function's domain

doc.summary: Computes the inverse tangent of `x` in radians.
doc.markdown:
Computes the inverse tangent of `x` in radians.
The result lies in `[-Pi / 2, Pi / 2]`. A signed zero returns itself, infinities approach the matching endpoint, and
a NaN remains a NaN.
doc.returns: the angle in radians whose tangent is `x`

doc.markdown: Computes the inverse tangent of `x` in radians at `float32` precision.
doc.returns: the angle in radians whose tangent is `x`

the answer lands in the subnormals. This steps in bounded pieces so neither happens: the result is correctly rounded

items.name: UlpDistance
items.signature: pub func UlpDistance(left: float64, right: float64) -> uint64

doc.summary: How many representable values lie between `left` and `right`.
doc.markdown:
How many representable values lie between `left` and `right`.
The natural way to state a floating-point error bound: two values are one ulp apart when nothing is representable
between them, and a function accurate to half an ulp returns the nearest representable value to the true answer.
Counting steps rather than subtracting is what makes the measure meaningful near zero, where the absolute difference
between neighbours is vanishingly small, and near the maximum, where it is enormous. Values of opposite sign are
counted through zero, with the two zeros treated as one value - the step from the smallest negative subnormal to the
smallest positive one is two, not three. A NaN in either argument has no distance and reports the largest `uint64`,
which no real distance can reach.
doc.returns: their distance in representable values, or the largest `uint64` when either is a NaN

doc.summary: The greatest common divisor of `left` and `right`, reporting whether it is representable.
doc.markdown:
The greatest common divisor of `left` and `right`, reporting whether it is representable.
Defined on magnitudes, so signs do not matter and the answer is never negative. `Gcd(0, 0)` is zero, which is the
conventional answer and the only one that keeps `Gcd(x, 0) == |x|` true everywhere. The single overflow is a divisor
equal to the magnitude of the most negative value - reachable only as `Gcd(min, 0)` and `Gcd(min, min)` - which no
signed type can express. Runs in time proportional to the number of bits and allocates nothing. `result` must be
non-null and writable.

doc.returns: `true` when the non-negative divisor is not representable as `T`

overflows readily - two coprime values multiply - so the flag is the usual case rather than the exception, and the
division is done before the multiplication so a representable answer is not lost to an intermediate that is not.

doc.markdown:
Raises `x` to the power `y`.
The error is at most one ulp. A negative base requires an integer exponent; otherwise the result is a NaN.
`PowInteger` is both faster and able to preserve exact results when the exponent is an integer.

items.signature: pub func PowInteger(base: float64, exponent: int64) -> float64

doc.summary: `base` raised to the integer power `exponent`.
doc.markdown:
`base` raised to the integer power `exponent`.
A zero exponent gives one for every base, including zero and a NaN, which is the same rule `Pow` follows: the empty
product is one. A negative exponent takes the reciprocal at the end rather than dividing as it goes, which keeps the
intermediates as large as possible and loses the least.
doc.returns: `base` raised to `exponent`

doc.summary: Rounds `x` to the nearest integral value, with halfway cases away from zero.
doc.markdown:
Rounds `x` to the nearest integral value, with halfway cases away from zero.
Thus `Round(2.5)` is `3.0` and `Round(-2.5)` is `-3.0`. The sign of zero is preserved, and a NaN or infinity passes
through unchanged. The fractional part is compared directly instead of adding one half, which avoids prematurely
rounding the largest representable value below `0.5` up to `1.0`.
doc.returns: the nearest integral value

cases.name: ToNearestTiesAway
cases.doc:
To the nearest, with a halfway value going away from zero: `Round`.
What most people mean by rounding, and what school teaches.

cases.name: ToNearestTiesEven
cases.doc:
To the nearest, with a halfway value going to the even neighbour.
IEEE 754's default, and the one that keeps a long run of roundings from drifting: ties away from zero rounds up
half the time and down never.

doc.summary: The nearest integer to `value`, with a halfway value going to the even neighbour.
doc.markdown:
The nearest integer to `value`, with a halfway value going to the even neighbour.
`RoundTiesToEven(2.5)` is 2 and `RoundTiesToEven(3.5)` is 4, where `Round` gives 3 and 4. The sign of a zero is
preserved, and a NaN or infinity passes through unchanged.
doc.returns: the nearest integral value, resolving halfway cases toward the even neighbour

items.signature: pub func ToIntegerChecked<T>(value: float64, sample: T, mode: RoundingMode, result: *var T) -> bool

doc.summary: `value` rounded in the named direction and converted to an integer, reporting whether it fits.
doc.markdown:
`value` rounded in the named direction and converted to an integer, reporting whether it fits.
`sample` is read by value and only its type matters, exactly as `Core`'s `MaximumOf` reads one. Returns `true` when
the rounded value is not representable in the integer type — because it is a NaN, an infinity, or simply out of
range — and leaves `result` zero in that case. This is the only place a float becomes an integer, and it refuses
rather than saturating, because a caller who has not thought about the out-of-range case is better served by a flag
than by a plausible wrong number. `result` must be non-null and writable.

params.name: result
params.markdown: receives the converted integer or zero on failure

doc.returns: `true` when the rounded value is not representable as `T`
